dimming.explanationTitle: Why does the star get dimmer?
dimming.explanation1: When a planet passes between its star and us, it covers a small part of the star. That part's light never reaches us, so the star looks a little dimmer. Astronomers call this a transit. The planets here circle a distant star: "Earth-sized" or "Jupiter-sized" only says how big they are.
dimming.explanation2: The bigger the planet compared with its star, the more light it blocks. A Jupiter-sized planet would block about 1 % of a Sun-like star's light; an Earth-sized planet only about 0.008 %, less than 1 part in 10 000.
dimming.explanation3: A small star makes the same planet easier to find: an Earth-sized planet in front of a red dwarf five times smaller than the Sun blocks 25 times more of the star's light.
dimming.explanation4: Real stars are so far away that telescopes see them as points. We never see the planet itself: we find it because its star dims, again and again, every time the planet goes around.
dimming.keyboardHelpMove: Move the planet along its orbit

liningUp.view3DTitle: The orbit and the direction to Earth

liningUp.chartTitle: The dip in the star's light
liningUp.ghostLegend: dashed: the same planet seen exactly edge-on
liningUp.randomSkyTitle: 100 stars like this one, tilted at random
liningUp.impactPattern: Passes {{value}} star radii from the center
liningUp.tiltLimitPattern: Transits only if the orbit is within {{value}}° of edge-on.
liningUp.probabilityPattern: Chance that a random orbit lines up: {{value}} %
liningUp.explanationTitle: Why don't we see every planet transit?
liningUp.explanation1: A planet blocks its star's light only if it passes between the star and us. That needs its orbit to be seen almost exactly edge-on.
liningUp.explanation2: Tilt the orbit a little and the planet crosses the star off-center: the transit gets shorter. Tilt it more and the planet only grazes the edge, then misses the star altogether.
liningUp.explanation3: Orbits point every which way, so only a fraction of planets transit for us: about the star's radius divided by the planet's distance. Planets close to their stars are far more likely to transit. Turn it around: an astronomer on a distant world would see our own Earth transit the Sun from only about 1 direction in 200.
liningUp.explanation4: That is why missions like Kepler and TESS watch hundreds of thousands of stars at once: to catch the few whose planets line up.

lightCurve.zoomChartTitle: One transit, zoomed in (all observed transits folded together)
lightCurve.limbDarkeningNote: The star's darker edge makes the middle of the dip deeper, so this radius comes out a little too big. Astronomers fit a model of the darkening.
lightCurve.lost: The dip is lost in the noise.
lightCurve.hint: A hint of a dip: observe more transits.
lightCurve.pointsReadoutPattern: {{points}} measurements inside the dip (one every {{cadence}} min)
lightCurve.equation: R<sub>planet</sub> = R<sub>star</sub> √depth    distance<sup>3</sup> = G M<sub>star</sub> P<sup>2</sup> ÷ 4π<sup>2</sup>    S/N = depth ÷ (σ ÷ √n)
lightCurve.explanation1: Depth: the fraction of light blocked is the planet's area divided by the star's, so the planet's radius is the star's radius times √depth. We know the star's size from its spectrum.
lightCurve.explanation2: Period: the time between dips is one orbit. With the star's mass, Kepler's third law turns it into the planet's distance from its star.
lightCurve.explanation3: Duration: how long the planet takes to cross the star. Far-out planets move slowly, so their transits last longer, but they come much less often.
lightCurve.explanation4: Noise: every measurement scatters a little. Folding many transits on top of each other and averaging shrinks the scatter by √n, so even an Earth-sized dip can stand out, given enough transits.

hunt.chartHint: Click a dip to mark it. Drag or scroll to move; wheel to zoom.
hunt.foldedHint: Folded: every point is placed by its time since the last predicted transit. Yellow: averages.
hunt.marksCountPattern: Dips marked: {{count}}. Mark at least two dips.
hunt.marksSpacingPattern: Dips marked: {{count}}; they repeat every {{spacing}} (dips missed in gaps allowed for).
hunt.answerSource: Colored ticks under the light curve show where each planet's transits are predicted.
hunt.explanation1: These are real measurements of real stars by NASA's Kepler and TESS space telescopes, cleaned of slow drifts and averaged into short bins. Each dot is the star's brightness at one moment.
hunt.explanation2: Find the period. Mark the dips you can see; the time between them is a first guess, even if a dip is lost in a gap in the data. Or tick Search for periods. Then fold the light curve: if the period is right, every dip lands on top of the others.
hunt.explanation3: Hidden planets. Some dips are smaller than the scatter of the points. Folding many transits together and averaging makes them appear, as with Kepler-10 b, Kepler's first rocky planet (2011).
hunt.explanation4: Measure the size. Drag the depth line to the bottom of the folded dip. With the star's radius, known from its spectrum, the depth gives the planet's radius. Then reveal what astronomers found.
hunt.searchHint: Click a peak to fold on it. Half and twice the period give echoes.
hunt.farSideAxis: Hours from half an orbit after the transit
hunt.explanation5: Searching by computer. The period search folds the light curve on thousands of trial periods and, for each one, slides a box along the fold to find the deepest dip. The height is how many times bigger than the noise that dip is. A planet makes a tall peak, with smaller echoes at half and twice its period. Kepler found most of its planets this way (the box least-squares method).
hunt.explanation6: The far side. Half an orbit after a transit, the planet passes behind its star. A hot Jupiter glows, so the light then dips a tiny bit more. Fold HAT-P-7 on its planet and tick Center on the far side: the averages dip by about 0.007 %, which is the planet's own light.

composition.depthPattern: The star dims by {{depth}} %. Star radius: {{starRadius}}.
composition.tiltPattern: Orbit tilt {{tilt}}°: almost edge-on, or there would be no transit.
composition.sizeCompare: Size compared with Earth and Jupiter:
composition.wobblePattern:
The star wobbles toward and away from us by ±{{k}} m/s, once every {{period}}. Star mass: {{starMass}}.
The wobble alone: at least {{minimum}}.
The transit says the orbit is almost edge-on, so the planet's mass is {{mass}}.
composition.timingPattern: This star's wobble is too small to measure. Instead, the planet's neighbors tug on it, so its transits come a few minutes early or late. Those timing changes give its mass: {{mass}}.
composition.rocky: Rocky, like Earth: rock and iron.
composition.inBetween: In between: too big for its mass to be bare rock, so it must have a thick layer of water or gas.
composition.giant: A gas giant, like Jupiter and Saturn: mostly hydrogen and helium.
composition.floats: Less dense than water: in a big enough bathtub, it would float!
composition.explanation1: A transit gives a planet's size. The star's wobble (see the Stellar Wobble simulation) gives its mass, but only a minimum, because we do not know how the orbit is tilted.
composition.explanation2: A planet that transits must have its orbit almost edge-on. So the transit removes the doubt: the minimum mass becomes the true mass.
composition.explanation3: Mass divided by volume is the density. Iron is about 8 g/cm³, rock about 3, water 1. Earth, with its iron core, averages 5.5. Gas giants are around 1 or less: Saturn would float in water.
composition.explanation4: On the mass–radius diagram, planets on the rocky curve are made of rock and iron; planets well above it must be wrapped in water or gas. Big planets get squeezed by their own gravity, so they are denser than their size alone suggests.
composition.stellarWobbleNote: You can measure this wobble yourself in Stellar Wobble's Observatory.
